questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How non-stick pans were invented by accident
Why politicians use social media to win votes
How to stop feeling embarrassed in public
The feeling of shame and whether it can be useful
questions.why: Neil and Sam discuss shame and whether it's always a bad thing.

questions.q: How has social media changed the idea of shame, according to the presenters?
options: It is now common to shame people publicly online
People feel much less shame than they did in the past
Shaming people is now banned on most social media sites
Only famous people and politicians feel shame now
questions.why: Sam says publicly shaming people is something we see a lot on social media.

questions.q: What does Hetta Howes think about shame?
options: It is always harmful and should be avoided
It is never useful in modern society
Too much is bad, but the right amount helps
Only young people should feel it at school
questions.why: She says too much is crippling, but the right amount can be really positive.

questions.q: Why can some shame be positive, according to Hetta Howes?
options: It makes people more popular
It can make people change their behaviour
It makes people work harder
It helps people forget mistakes
questions.why: She says it 'effects change', so publicly shaming someone may bring positive change.

questions.q: Which group does Neil suggest has to accept public shaming more than others?
options: Teachers
Journalists
Scientists
Politicians
questions.why: Sam guesses politicians, and Neil goes on to talk about them.

questions.q: What does Tiffany Watt-Smith mean by a 'Teflon-coated politician'?
options: A politician who criticism and shame don't affect
A politician who works in the cooking industry
A politician who is very popular
A politician who always tells the truth
questions.why: Sam explains criticism and shame just don't stick to some politicians.

questions.q: How does Tiffany Watt-Smith feel about someone who never feels shame?
options: She admires them
She thinks it's frightening
She finds it funny
She thinks it's normal
questions.why: She calls it 'a kind of frightening image'.

questions.q: Why does Neil ask about non-stick cooking pans at the start?
options: Sam asked him to at the start of the show
The programme was going to be about cooking
It links to the Teflon image of politicians
It was a random question with no real link
questions.why: He promised 'all will become clear', and Teflon later describes some politicians.
